BAE Systems has ramped up its acquisition efforts, purchasing six more companies
Nurturing its United States presence is a major element of BAE Systems
BAE Systems North America is well positioned to benefit from the rise in U.S. defense spending

BAE Systems North America was created in November 1999 via the merger of British Aerospace North America and Marconi North America, as part of the $12.7 billion merger of British Aerospace and Marconi Electronic Systems.  The deal gave BAE Systems a tremendous footprint in the U.S.  market thanks to the earlier Marconi acquisitions of several U.S. aerospace and defense companies such as Lear Astronics, Hazeltine, Tracor, Reflectone, General Dynamics Electronics Division, and GEC-Marconi.

In addition, BAE Systems North America was further enhanced with the late 2000 acquisitions of Lockheed Martin Control Systems and Lockheed Martin Aerospace Electronics Systems, which consisted of Sanders, Fairchild Systems, and Lockheed Martin Space & Electronics Systems.
Today, BAE Systems North America ranks as a top U.S. DoD defense contractor with operations in 30 states, and employs more than 23,000 people.
Senior Vice President, Legal & General Counsel
BAE Systems North America is an operational group of the U.K.-based BAE Systems.  The unit is structured as follows:

Platform Solutions.  Platform Solutions is a major producer of control systems and subsystems for air, space, water, and ground vehicles for civilian and military markets.  The unit manufactures a wide range of subsystems, including fly-by-wire flight controls, digital autopilots and flight directors, full-authority digital engine controls, navigation guidance systems, launch vehicle controls, UAV systems, low-visibility precision landing systems, and integrated avionics.  The sector also provides hybrid-electric drive systems for intra-city transit buses and other medium and large vehicles.

Information & Electronic Systems Integration.  This sector produces electronic warfare and self-protection systems; tactical surveillance and intelligence systems; microwave systems; mission and space electronics; infrared systems; C4I systems integration; and communication, navigation, identification, and reconnaissance systems.  Other key products include avionics systems; military and industrial displays; combat identification systems; night vision head-up displays and beacons; Doppler navigation systems; advanced Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) systems for ground, ship, and airborne applications; SATCOM communications; space systems and subsystems; and chemical agent detection devices.  This unit also is responsible for air structure assembly and aircraft and avionics modernization; flight testing, certification and operations; and development and manufacture of full- or sub-scale aerial targets.

Technology Solutions.  This segment provides systems engineering and integration services to the Navy, Air Force, Army, and other customers in the areas of communications systems; undersea, anti-air, and strike warfare combat systems; air traffic control and identification systems; strategic weapons systems; ship systems design and engineering; transportation systems; and space systems.  The unit is also responsible for managing the operation of the Holston Army Ammunition Plant in Kingsport, Tennessee.

Information Systems.  This unit provides information technology products, systems, and services to the U.S. Department of Defense, non-defense government agencies, and the commercial market.  Products include test equipment for space launch vehicles, space avionics, satellites, telecommunications, and training systems.

In terms of everyday business, BAE Systems North America
s products, systems, and services are sold primarily to the U.S. defense marketplace.  BAE Systems ranked 13th among U.S. Department of Defense prime contractors for 2003.
Thermal Weapon Sight.  In April 2004, BAE Systems was awarded a five-year multiyear contract by the U.S. Army

s Communication and Electronics Command (CECOM) to supply a family of next-generation thermal weapon sights for its soldiers.  The base contract is worth $111 million, and could be valued at more than $250 million if all options are exercised.  The thermal weapon sight (TWS) will be developed in partnership with Team Soldier at Fort Belvoir, Virginia, and will provide the U.S. Army Infantry with the ability to detect and engage targets day or night, in all weather and battlefield obscurant conditions.  The TWS enables individual and crew-served weapon gunners to see deep into the battlefield, increasing their surveillance and target acquisition range.  The TWS will be produced at BAE Systems facility in Lexington, Massachusetts.

APKWS.  In March 2003, General Dynamics Armament and Technical Products (ATP) awarded BAE Systems a $26.7 million contract for the development and demonstration of the guidance section of the U.S. Army

s Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) Block I program.  The contract was finalized March 13, 2003, with BAE Systems Information & Electronic Warfare Systems (IEWS), in Nashua, New Hampshire.  APKWS is a low-cost precision munition that is highly accurate and effective against soft to lightly armored targets.  The BAE Systems guidance section provides pinpoint accuracy for the Army
enough to home in on and destroy enemy targets while minimizing collateral damage.

IDECM.  In March 2001, the U.S. Navy awarded a $59 million contract to BAE Systems for low-rate initial production of an integrated defensive electronic countermeasures/radio frequency countermeasures system that will be deployed initially on Navy F/A
18E/F aircraft, and followed by U.S. Air Force B

1B and F-15 aircraft.  Under Phase I of the contract, the Information & Electronic Warfare Systems business unit of BAE Systems North America will deliver six onboard systems and 30 fiber-optic towed decoys, plus spares.  An option for Phase II would provide an additional 14 onboard systems, 30 fiber-optic towed decoys, spares, and provisions for foreign military sales.  Total value of the contract, including options, could reach $145 million.

Naval Surface Warfare Center Support.  In January 2001, BAE Systems won a $63.7 million, five-year contract from the U.S. Navy to provide quality high-tech engineering services in support of technical programs at the Naval Surface Warfare Center.  BAE Systems Applied Technologies, part of BAE Systems North America, will provide technical and engineering services at the Center

s Dahlgren division in Virginia to support a wide array of U.S. Navy and Marine Corps programs, including missiles, launchers, guns, munitions, and test and evaluation programs.  Work will focus particularly on program management, systems engineering, configuration/data management, technical documentation, engineering and information environments, specialty engineering, integrated logistics support, quality assurance, and test and evaluation.

Platform Solutions Sector Formed.  In April 2003, BAE Systems North America formed a new operating sector that combines controls and avionics capabilities to serve a broad range of military and commercial platforms, from ground vehicles to airplanes to spacecraft.  The new Platform Solutions sector includes the existing BAE Systems Controls business and will have operational control of the company
s Avionic Systems Division in Rochester and Edinburgh, U.K.

The new sector develops and produces electronic vehicle management systems, engine controls, cockpit and helmet displays, and inertial systems for a variety of platforms including fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft, missiles, ground vehicles, ships, and space launch vehicles.  Headquartered in Johnson City, it employs approximately 6,400 people at 12 facilities in the United States and the United Kingdom.

Imaging Sensors Unit Spun Off.  In April 2001, BAE Systems North America reached agreement with the Carlyle Group, Washington, D.C., to spin off its Imaging Sensors business located at Milpitas, California.  Imaging Sensors was previously part of BAE Systems Reconnaissance and Surveillance Systems of Syosset, New York.  In the transaction, BAE Systems has provided the assets of Imaging Sensors to form a new company, Fairchild Imaging Inc.  The agreement closed on April 6, 2001.  The new company employs 123 people.  Under the terms of the transaction, BAE Systems North America retains an equity interest in Fairchild Imaging.  The new company will continue to provide camouflage, concealment, and deception products to the Reconnaissance and Surveillance Systems business within BAE Systems North America.  Financial terms were not disclosed.

STI Government Systems Acquired.  In May 2004, BAE Systems North America completed its acquisition of Honolulu-based STI Government Systems for $27 million in cash.  The transaction complements BAE Systems technology in photonics, information technologies, and systems integration.  STI Government Systems employs 125 people.  The unit will be called BAE Systems Spectral Solutions and will operate within the company
s CNIR business unit.  CNIR is headquartered in Wayne, New Jersey.  The deal was first announced in April 2004.

Acoustics Systems Facility Sold.  In November 2003, BAE Systems North America completed the sale of its acoustics systems facility, located in Braintree, Massachusetts.  The negotiated $10 million cash sale to Ultra Electronics Holdings plc (Ultra) was originally announced in September 2003.  Ocean Systems has 80 employees who produce special purpose acoustic and RF devices and systems for submarines, surface ships, and acoustic test ranges.

Advanced Power Technologies Acquired.  In March 2003, BAE Systems North America completed its acquisition of Washington, D.C.-based Advanced Power Technologies Inc (APTI), following receipt of regulatory approval.  The $27 million cash transaction complements BAE Systems

intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance exploitation, and information processing for defense, civil, and commercial uses.  The 17-year-old APTI changed its name to BAE Systems Advanced Technologies, a fully integrated organization operating within the company
s Information & Electronic Warfare Systems business unit.  APTI

s core competencies include RF and optical engineering, communications and networking, signal and data exploitation, and knowledge creation.  The new unit has facilities in Virginia, Maryland, and Alaska and employs more than 100 people.  In 2002, it had revenues of approximately $26 million.

MEVATEC Acquisition Completed.  In March 2003, BAE Systems North America completed its acquisition of MEVATEC Corporation of Huntsville, Alabama, for $82 million in cash.  MEVATEC is a fast-growing provider of professional technical services to the Department of Defense; civilian, federal, state, and local government agencies; and commercial businesses.  MEVATEC is positioned in missile defense, joint interoperability, outsourcing, and business process re-engineering.  In addition to its headquarters in Huntsville, MEVATEC has facilities in 13 other locations across the United States and employs 500 people.  MEVATEC had 2002 revenues of approximately $120 million.  MEVATEC Corporation changed its name to BAE Systems Analytical Solutions, and operates as a business unit within BAE Systems Technology Solutions sector.

Condor Pacific Acquired.  In December 2002, BAE Systems North America completed its acquisition of Condor Pacific Industries Inc, Westlake Village, California, a producer of sensors and guidance systems for the aerospace industry, following receipt of all regulatory approvals.  The $58.5 million acquisition will strengthen BAE Systems activities in guidance and control of military systems.  The Condor Pacific business, which also includes plant locations in Cheshire, Connecticut; and Heath, Ohio, will be part of BAE Systems Controls Sector.
Corbbet Technologies Acquired.  In November 2002, BAE Systems North America completed its acquisition of Corbett Technologies Inc for $15 million in cash.  The transaction complements BAE Systems

established information technology and secure information businesses.  Corbett Technologies, based in Alexandria, Virginia, and employing more than 100 people, focuses on safeguarding information systems by providing full-service Information Assurance solutions.

BAE Systems Sells Gaithersburg Operation.  In September 2002, BAE Systems North America and Integrated Defense Technologies reached a definitive agreement under which Integrated Defense Technologies Inc will acquire BAE Systems Advanced Systems

operation located in Gaithersburg, Maryland.  Employing 300-plus workers, the unit designs and manufactures high-performance radio frequency surveillance equipment used in signals intelligence applications.  The deal was valued at $146 million.

Chaff and Flare Business Sold.  In August 2002, BAE Systems North America completed the sale of its expendable defensive countermeasures business, located in Lillington, North Carolina, and East Camden, Arkansas.  The negotiated $67.5 million cash sale to Esterline Technologies was originally announced July 15.  At the Lillington facility, about 65 employees produce radar countermeasure chaff used by aircraft to help protect against radar-guided missiles.  At East Camden, about 235 employees produce a variety of aircraft-dispensable flares designed to protect against infrared-guided missiles.

CCD Business Sold to Saab.  In April 2002, BAE Systems North America completed the sale of its Camouflage, Concealment, and Deception (CCD) business, located at Lillington, North Carolina.  The sale, to Saab Barracuda LLC, was originally announced on March 11, 2002; closing of the sale followed completion of its review by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS).  Terms of the deal were not announced.

BAE Systems Canada Stake Sold.  In February 2001, BAE Systems announced an agreement to sell its approximately 54 percent majority investment in BAE Systems Canada (formerly Canadian Marconi Company) to ONCAP LP, an investment firm located in Toronto, Canada, for $398.1 million.  The deal was consummated in late April 2001 when ONCAP successfully completed the acquisition of all of the common shares of BAE Systems Canada Inc.  BAE Systems Canada will now conduct business under the new name CMC Electronics Inc.  CMC Electronics will specialize in the design, manufacture, sale, and support of high-technology electronic products.  These products include avionics, aircraft satellite communications antennas, specialized electronic components, military radios, space electronics, infrared cameras, medium- and high-end global positioning systems, and marine electronics.  The divestiture is the largest deal to date by BAE Systems as it seeks to streamline and integrate its businesses.

BAE Completes Sanders Purchase.  In November 2000, BAE Systems North America completed its acquisition of Lockheed Martin Aerospace Electronics Systems (AES) in a $1.67 billion cash transaction.  AES is composed of Sanders, Fairchild Systems, and the Space Electronics & Communications businesses with principal facilities in New Hampshire, New York, and Virginia.  Major AES products include aircraft self-protection systems, tactical surveillance and intelligence systems, reconnaissance and navigation systems, automated mission-planning systems, microwave electronics, infrared sensors, and radiation-hardened digital components and systems for space applications.  The AES businesses, with approximately 5,000 employees, had net sales for the first nine months of 2000 of approximately $510 million, excluding intercompany sales.  Current backlog for the AES businesses is approximately $1.2 billion.  AES became BAE Systems Information & Electronic Systems Integration sector, a wholly owned subsidiary of BAE Systems

The acquisition received final clearance in November 2000 when the Pentagon and the Department of Defense notified the companies that they had no national security objections to the sale of U.K.-based BAE Systems.  Officials in the U.S. Department of Defense, the British Embassy, and industry have told Forecast International that a thorough investigation of security procedures found no problems.  Recently at the British Embassy, a BAE official explained how dealing with major security issues from either side of the Atlantic was familiar territory for the company and isolating different departments that were working with prime contractors on opposite sides of a bid had become standard.  Managers were restricted from finding out competitive or proprietary information from opposing bidding teams, something of concern at the Pentagon.
BAE Acquires Control Systems.  In April 2000, BAE Systems North America announced that it would purchase Lockheed Martin
s Control Systems Division for $510 million.  The acquisition will complement BAE Systems

established electronic systems and flight-controls systems businesses.  Control Systems has particular strengths in full-authority digital engine controls (FADEC) and digital fly-by-wire flight controls with a broad range of program applications.  The deal was completed in September 2000.

Marconi Actuation Sold.  In February 2000, BAE Systems North America signed a definitive agreement to sell its Marconi Actuation Systems Inc subsidiary to Smiths Industries Aerospace for $100 million.  Actuation Systems, located in Whippany, New Jersey, designs, engineers, and services various electromechanical motion-control systems for commercial and military aircraft.  Actuation Systems was sold primarily because the motion-control business lies outside BAE Systems
strategic focus and core competencies of electronics, information technology, and systems engineering and integration.

Femtometrics Acquired.  In February 2000, BAE Systems North America acquired Femtometrics, an Irvine, California, technology company specializing in chemical agent detection.  Femtometrics and BAE Systems have been teamed on the Tri-Service Joint Chemical Agent Detector (JCAD) program, which provides an accurate, reliable, and low-cost personal detector for military personnel in aircraft, armor, vessel, and ground installations.  Terms of the deal were not disclosed.

WJ Telecommunications Unit Acquired.  In January 2000, BAE Systems North America acquired the Watkins-Johnson Telecommunications Group for an undisclosed amount.  The unit specializes in signal surveillance and military communications.  Headquartered in Gaithersburg, Maryland, the Telecommunications Group produces radio frequency electronic products and state-of-the-art equipment for applications in communications surveillance, direction finding, and signal processing for the U.S. DoD and prime contractors.  The group will now be known as Gaithersburg Operations, and will be organized as a unit of the Aerospace Electronics division of BAE Systems North America. s defense industrial base at the prime systems integration level.  Officials feel that without the transfer of technology, the U.K. will not have the skills necessary to support, maintain, or upgrade common weapon systems such as the Joint Strike Fighter on which it is partnered.
